456.t: Heifetz demands more basses in the Beethoven concerto
456.s: Heifetz, rehearsing the Beethoven violin concerto in Indianapolis, insists the basses play louder than Sevitzky allowed, saying it is his concerto and Beethoven wrote it.
456.q: Oh, yes. And how? Heifetz played many times. I remember, he used to come every year. In fact, I remember one year, we're scheduled to do a Beethoven violin concerto. And, uh, of course, uh, Szyzki always had to rehearse the orchestra part first. Very important, you know. I remember one time, he…

456.t: Playing under Stokowski and the Mardi Gras walk-off
456.s: He finally played with Stokowski in New Orleans, where the conductor walked off during El Amor Brujo because of a Mardi Gras ball's noise next door; he admires Stokowski's phrasing.
456.q: Oh, it sounds good. I wonder if that's coming through the tape. I hope so. Yeah. Oh, you go ahead. Some more. After you. Okay. Yes, I did play with Leopold. And, uh, well, that was a long time ago. I'm noble. It took me a long time before I did get to play with Leopold, because, as a matter of…

456.t: Massimo Freccia, the New Orleans Symphony conductor
456.s: Freccia was personally nice but struggled to explain what he wanted in English; Mazzari, as librarian, knew him better than most players.
456.q: Well, Massimo Freccia was a very nice person, personally. I mean, he was. He's conducting in Italy now, you know. In fact, I came in the same year he came in. And, uh, I was a record librarian. That's how I got to know Massimo Freccia a little better than the average musician in the orchestra…

456.t: Alexander Hilsberg and conductors who pick on players
456.s: Hilsberg, a former Philadelphia concertmaster, did not pick on him and greeted players asking if they had practiced; Mazzari then reflects on conductors who stop the orchestra to cover being lost.
456.q: Oh, Alexander Hillsberg. He's conducting the orchestra right now, huh? Well, I played on the Hillsberg full season and then I was only called in as extra strings were needed. But fortunately, uh, I, Hillsberg was one of the conductors who didn't pick on me and we got along real fine together. He,…

456.s: He lists soloists he accompanied and recalls Milstein sitting in the second violins at rehearsal and coming in wrong, to everyone's laughter.
456.q: Oh, yes. Of course. Oh, I can't remember all of them. A lot of violinists, cellists, sopranos, you know, like, ooh, Sigeti, Heifetz, Francescati. Well, naturally, anyone who does play in a symphony orchestra gets to see all those people, you know.

457.s: He praises Everett Lee, who conducted for Carmen Jones, and has tried to get him a Grant Park date.
457.q: Well, there are a lot of... Among the newcomers that I admire greatly and have all the respect in the world for them on various instruments. There's a young fella I met about four or five years ago. He's originally from Cleveland. He's living in New York now. Violinist by the name of Everett Lee.…

281.t: Fritz Reiner and the New York Philharmonic
281.s: Reiner came to hear him at Nick's, invited him to a Philharmonic rehearsal, and liked his big sound; Spanier calls him a human perfectionist.
281.q: Well, Fritz Reiner, when he'd come to New York to direct the Philharmonic, he'd always come down to Nick's to hear me play. And, uh, one day he asked me to, if I'd like to come to rehearsal for Philharmonic. I said, sure. And he said, well, bring your horn too.

458.s: Beal praises Bernstein's pulse, recalls works played with him, and discusses distrust of conductors without a beat and Broadway pit conductors.
458.q: Really he had the beat man. He had a great pulse. And he didn’t have to convey it, it was just there you know. It was there. And I played a couple of things with him. I played on a mass that he wrote, a recording, I played actually Fender bass on that. And there was a ballet piece he wrote called…

323.t: Toscanini and Stokowski and the Shostakovich Seventh
323.s: Premiering the Shostakovich Seventh on a borrowed low-C bass clarinet, under both conductors.
323.q: Stokowski. Well let me tell you about the two conductors. They used to alternate. One week on the broadcast Toscanini conducted. The next week Stokowski. And they alternated. Now we premiered the Shostakovitch Seventh Symphony. It can be bought. It was taken off the air. And I had to borrow a…

338.t: Nights at Condon's and Leonard Bernstein's City Center Symphony
338.s: Condon's was a boozy, lively room where Bernstein and David Diamond came in; Bernstein suggested he audition for the City Center Symphony, which he did in his second year.
338.ch: New York, NBC and Eddie Condon's
338.q: Well you had to be in pretty good shape to take it you know, because there was plenty of drinking going on there, and smoking cigarettes and what have you. There was a lot of action going on there all the time, but it was fun and all the musicians came in there. And I met Leonard Bernstein there.…

459.t: Dispute with a classical conductor on West Side Story dances
459.s: A conductor mis-explained jazz eighths at a New York Philharmonic Bernstein birthday piece; Shiner and Walter Rosenberger recorded it in two takes.
459.q: I had one, which I quoted, it was written up in the Rochester jazz paper, where they did dances from “West Side Story,” which I premiered with the New York Philharmonic in New York. And the conductor, it was a birthday present for Lenny Bernstein. I won’t name the conductor, but he stopped and he…

460.t: Conductors at the Met: Bernstein, Karajan and Wagner
460.s: Laws lists the conductors he worked under and says he prized Bernstein's dramatic Romantic readings and loves Wagner's operas.
460.ch: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
460.q: strong name in conducting, and Zubin Mehta. James Levine is still there. Leonard Bernstein. I’m just trying to think of some of the orchestra conductors that came through that I was able to work with. Good experience, because those names – I don’t hear too much about other names nowadays that are…
